analysis.one_liner: Restricts payday-style small-dollar lenders' access to borrowers' bank accounts and blocks overdraft fees on prepaid cards.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in November 2022, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened rules on small-dollar, payday-style lending. It would let consumers block "remotely created checks" — checks drawn on their bank account without their signature — and stop automatic electronic withdrawals when repaying a loan. Small-dollar lenders would have to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, follow the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives (closing a loophole for online lenders), and companies that sell borrowers' personal financial data to lenders would face new restrictions. It would also ban overdraft fees on prepaid cards and require a government study of small-dollar lending's effects on tribal members.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income borrowers who use payday-style loans, prepaid cards, or online lenders. The bill would give them the right to stop lenders from repeatedly pulling money from their bank accounts, block unauthorized checks drawn on their accounts, cap fees by their home state's laws, and shield their personal financial information from data brokers feeding the payday loan industry.

how_it_helps.text: Remotely created checks — checks drawn on a consumer's account without their signature — could only be issued by a person the consumer had designated in writing and given to their bank, and consumers could revoke that designation at any time.
Consumers repaying small-dollar loans by electronic fund transfer would gain the right to stop payment, ending the practice of lenders repeatedly withdrawing from borrowers' accounts.

Small-dollar lenders would have to register with the CFPB before issuing credit, and loans made over the internet or by national banks would have to comply with the interest-rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing the loophole lenders used to export high rates.

Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts would be prohibited, and companies that broker or arrange payday loan applications could no longer collect and resell borrowers' sensitive financial information unless they directly made the loan.

analysis.who_pays: Payday and other small-dollar lenders, lead-generation companies that sell borrowers' financial data, and prepaid card issuers who collect overdraft fees. Their revenue and business models depend on the practices the bill restricts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and prepaid card issuers

drawbacks.text: Applying home-state rate caps to loans made over the internet or by national banks could reduce the availability of legal small-dollar credit in states with strict rate limits, pushing some borrowers toward unregulated or offshore lenders.

The registration, state-law, and lead-generation rules add compliance costs for small-dollar lenders, which some argue would be passed on to borrowers or drive lenders out of the market in states where the product is legal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target real, well-documented harms: repeated overdraft fees, unauthorized account withdrawals via remotely created checks, and out-of-state payday loans that dodge state rate caps. The costs fall on a concentrated industry rather than on taxpayers, though consumers could lose access to fast small-dollar credit in states with strict rate caps. On balance the benefits to consumers outweigh the industry's losses, and the bill's modest scope makes even that tradeoff limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in November 2022, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 16, 2022 — seven weeks before the 117th Congress ended — and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote.
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, all unfinished bills died, so the bill never came to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small-dollar lenders, lead brokers, and prepaid-card issuers kept the status quo — they never had to register, submit to home-state rate caps, or stop overdraft fees, and consumers gained no new protections.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 10 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans signed on.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 16, 2022 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-held committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force registration with the CFPB, apply each borrower's home-state interest-rate and fee laws to online and bank-issued loans, and stop automatic account withdrawals. It directly attacks the fee-and-refinance model that makes small-dollar lending highly profitable.

industries.industry: Lead generators and online loan brokers
industries.note: These companies harvest borrowers' Social Security and bank account numbers and sell them to payday lenders; the bill would bar them from doing so unless they directly make the loan themselves.
The bill bans overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, a fee stream largely paid by low-income consumers who use prepaid cards instead of bank accounts.
